title: Why I Chose English for My Content
content: Before I made my first video, the hardest decision wasn’t about gear, software, or editing. It was something much simpler and much more annoying: which language should I create content in? The obvious answer was Slovenian. It’s my mother tongue, and when you’re just starting out, going after your home market first feels like the safe move. But Slovenia is small — and small means limited reach. No matter how good the content is, you’re capped from day one. English, on the other hand, felt like jumping into an ocean that was already full of fish. Thousands of creators, hundreds covering the same topics — I’d just be another voice in the noise. Then it clicked: I’m my own person. I see the world in my own way, and I usually do things a little differently. One more voice in the ocean only disappears into it if it sounds like all the others. So English it is — and every now and then I’ll throw a Slovene word into the mix, just to see who perks up. Content creation isn’t a side quest for me — it’s the route I want to take. Tech is where I’m most at home: networks, systems, hardware, the homelab. But I don’t want to be locked into how-to videos forever. The first video is already out just to break the ice, more are planned, and there’s a growing list of topics waiting to be made. The goal is to share my view on things, and how I think they should be. I’m not trying to be the Slovenian Linus Tech Tips. I’d rather share, gather like-minded people, and build a real community around the things I’m genuinely into. Money? Sure, if it comes — I won’t turn it down. But I’ve always seen YouTube as something more than that. It’s a place where people can look back years later and see how things were at some point in time — and how much we improved as people, right alongside how much the technology improved. If building something together sounds like your thing, the Discord is where I hang out.

title: Hello World from AI
content: This is my very first post created entirely through an AI assistant. It all started with me asking a simple question - whether the AI could write posts for this blog for me. Turns out, it can. All I had to do was: Provide access to this repository Explain the topic I wanted to write about Let the assistant figure out the markdown format by looking at my existing posts The assistant cloned the repo, studied the format of my previous posts, and created this file following the exact same syntax. It even pushed it automatically so the GitHub Pages workflow picked it up. A quick thought on that: it feels a bit surreal to have software write the story of how software helped me write. But so far it works great, and it makes blogging a lot easier than firing up VS Code every time. More posts to come soon.

title: Dual PC Streaming - No extra hardware required
content: A dual PC streaming setup doesn’t have to start with an expensive capture card. In this video I walk through the whole process of getting your gaming and streaming machines working together — using NDI over your local network instead of a capture card. Quick note on what this covers We go end to end, from the hardware you actually need to the software that ties it together: Hardware requirements — what both PCs need, and why you probably already have it How to connect everything — the cabling and network basics NDI setup on the gaming PC — sending the feed over your LAN NDI setup on the streaming PC — receiving it and taking over the encoding load OBS Studio setup — getting your scenes and encoder ready on the streaming side OBS NDI plugin — the piece that makes the two machines talk to each other Microphone setup — routing your mic from the streaming PC to the gaming PC Final thoughts — what I’d do differently The result is a second PC that owns all the streaming work, so your gaming PC can focus on gaming — without spending a cent on a capture card. Watch it here: Dual PC Streaming Setup - The easiest way possible (no capture card needed)! Also join the Discord if you have questions about your own setup.

title: Network Cheat Sheet
content: Twisted Pair Cables Cheat-Sheet Cable Types Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) As the title states, a UTP cable has no shielding. This is the most used and most basic type of cable. The cable contains pairs of wires twisted together to help reduce and prevent electromagnetic interference. Shielded Twisted Pair (STP) STP cables are similar to UTP cables, where the wires are twisted together and then wrapped with a shielding or screening material which consits of foil wrapping or a copper braid jacket. Foil Twisted Pair (FTP) With FTP cables, each twisted pair of cables is wrapped in a shielding of foil to protect the cable from EMI and crosstalk. Shielded Foil Twisted Pair (S/FTP) A cable that is classified as S/FTP or Shielded Foil Twisted Pair is a combination of both FTP and STP shielding. The wires inside the cable are twisted and then shielded with a foil wrapping, then the 4-pair grouping of foiled wires are shielded by a wrapping of either foil or a flexible braided screening. This provides the highest level of protection against EMI and crosstalk. Wiring TIA/EIA 568AWiring Color Color Text 1. White and Green White and Green 2. Green Green 3. title: Windows 11
content: Most useful settings worth changing on a freshly installed Windows 11 Restore the classic right-click context menu 1. Open Regedit by hitting the Windows key and typing regedit. Hit Enter to launch it. 2. Navigate to HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Classes\CLSID 3. Right-click > New > Key, and paste in this name: {86ca1aa0-34aa-4e8b-a509-50c905bae2a2} 4. With the new key you just created highlighted, again right-click > New > Key, and paste in this name: InprocServer32 5. Double-click the (Default) registry entry and then hit Enter without typing anything to set its value to blank. Before making this change, you’ll see under the Data column that it says (value not set), but once you hit Enter it’ll show nothing. 6. Close Registry Editor. To see your new (classic) context menu, either restart your computer or open Task Manager, scroll down to the Windows Explorer process, and right-click > End task. Then File > Run new task and type explorer.exe to restart the Windows explorer process. And there you go: context menus changed! Fix slow first launch of VLC Solution A VLCwin7User on the VideoLan forums came up a solution that I will paraphrase and add to: Bring up an administrative command prompt in the vlc.exe directory. This would typically be C:\Program Files (x86)\VideoLAN\VLC for 32-bit, or C:\Program Files\VideoLan\VLC for 64-bit. (To bring up an administrative prompt in this directory, open the Start menu and type cmd. Right click on Command Prompt and select Run as administrator. Then type cd, space, and then the VLC directory, and press enter.) Issue vlc-cache-gen .\plugins and press enter… which generates \plugins\plugins.dat This brought launch time down to less than a second on my machine. Solution B This is the solution I had originally tried, but it only reduced the launch time by about 25%. I’m putting it here for completeness. I did not notice this making much difference after using Solution A above. Open VLC preferences via the menu or by pressing Ctrl + P. Select show settings > All from the bottom left corner In the Advanced section, uncheck “Scan for new plugins” Find images by specific resolution Open Windows Explorer and search for: width:<800 height:<600 Shortcut to network settings Create a shortcut on the Desktop and paste in: rundll32.exe shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL ncpa.cpl Afterwards you can pin it to Start, open location of the Start icon and pin to taskbar Add a network device to the Windows Defender exclusion list Run PowerShell as Admin Enter: -inputformat none -outputformat none -NonInteractive -Command Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "\raspberrypi\NAS" PS C:\Windows\system32>
